title: Configuration: Ring + Interior Structure
content: A Configuration packages two natural numbers: ringSize (the boundary cycle length) and interiorSize (vertices inside the ring), with the constraint ringSize ≥ 2. This matches the mathematical definition: a configuration is a planar graph where the outer face boundary forms a cycle of length ringSize. Reducibility is then about whether a proper 4-coloring of the ring cycle can always be extended to the interior. IsReducible is currently stubbed as True — the actual definition requires enumerating ring colorings and checking extension.
mathContext: A configuration $C = (G, \gamma)$ consists of a planar graph $G$ with outer face boundary $\gamma$ (the 'ring' of size $r$). $C$ is reducible if for every proper 4-coloring of the ring $\gamma$, the coloring extends to a proper 4-coloring of all of $G$. Checking this requires examining $\leq 3^r/r$ essentially different ring colorings.

title: Birkhoff Diamond: First Reducible Configuration (1913)
content: The Birkhoff diamond (ringSize=6, interiorSize=4) is the simplest non-trivial reducible configuration, discovered by George Birkhoff in 1913. It consists of a hexagonal ring with 4 interior vertices forming a diamond shape. Birkhoff showed that any 4-coloring of the 6-vertex ring can be extended to the 4 interior vertices, which was a key step toward the eventual proof of the Four Color Theorem. The diamond has the smallest ring size of any known reducible configuration.
mathContext: The Birkhoff diamond has ring size 6 and is the only reducible configuration with ring size $\leq 5$ (rings of size $\leq 5$ are not reducible). Birkhoff's 1913 paper introduced the configuration/reducibility framework and proved this configuration reducible using the theory of Kempe chains.

title: Unavoidability via Discharging
content: IsUnavoidable S says every 5-connected planar graph contains a member of S (currently stubbed as True). In practice, unavoidability is proved by the *discharging method*: assign charges 6-deg(v) to each vertex and 6-|f| to each face. By Euler's formula for planar graphs, the total charge is exactly 12 > 0. Discharging rules redistribute charges; if the configuration set S is unavoidable, some element must appear, contradicting the assumption that all charges become ≤ 0.
mathContext: Euler's formula: $V - E + F = 2$. For a planar triangulation: $\sum_v (6 - \deg v) + \sum_f (6 - |f|) = 12$. After discharging (redistributing charges by fixed rules), if $S$ is unavoidable, every 5-connected planar graph contains a member of $S$. The total positive charge proves at least one must occur.

title: Historical Reduction: 1936 → 1476 → 633 Configurations
content: The configuration count tracks the progress of computer-assisted proofs. Appel-Haken (1977) used 1936 configurations in their original proof — the first major computer-assisted proof, requiring months of CPU time. They reduced it to 1476 in the same year. Robertson-Sanders-Seymour-Thomas (1997) achieved 633 with a cleaner discharging proof and more efficient reducibility checking. Gonthier (2008) formally verified the RSST proof in Coq. The minimum unknown set size is the outstanding open question.
mathContext: The computational cost of checking reducibility scales as $O(\text{(ring-colorings)} \times \text{(extension checks)}) \sim O(3^r)$ for ring size $r$. Reducing configuration count often means accepting larger ring sizes, creating a trade-off. RSST achieved 633 with ring sizes up to 11.

title: The Open Question: Minimum Configuration Set
content: The open question documents three obstacles to reducing below 633: (1) computational: reducibility checking is exponential in ring size, (2) unavoidability: removing a configuration requires adjusting discharging rules, potentially adding others, (3) trade-off: fewer configurations often means larger rings. Heuristic estimates suggest ~200-400 configurations suffice, but no tight lower bound is known. The file notes this is heuristic rather than proved — an honest assessment of the mathematical state of the art.
mathContext: A lower bound argument would need to show that for any set $S$ of fewer than $k$ configurations, either some configuration fails reducibility or some planar graph avoids all of $S$. No such bound tighter than ~10 is currently proved. The heuristic estimate of 200-400 comes from the structure of the discharging rules in the RSST proof.
